> Day.js is a minimalist JavaScript library that parses, validates, manipulates, and displays dates and times for modern browsers with a largely Moment.js-compatible API. If you use Moment.js, you already know how to use Day.js. ```js dayjs().startOf('month').add(1, 'day').set('year', 2018).format('YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss'); ``` * 🕒 Familiar Moment.js API & patterns * 💪 Immutable * 🔥 Chainable * 🌐 I18n support * 📦 2kb mini library * 👫 All browsers supported --- ## Getting Started ### Documentation You can find more details, API, and other docs on [day.js.org](https://day.js.org/) website. ### Installation ```console npm install dayjs --save ``` 📚[Installation Guide](https://day.js.org/docs/en/installation/installation) ### API It's easy to use Day.js APIs to parse, validate, manipulate, and display dates and times. ```javascript dayjs('2018-08-08') // parse dayjs().format('{YYYY} MM-DDTHH:mm:ss SSS [Z] A') // display dayjs().set('month', 3).month() // get & set dayjs().add(1, 'year') // manipulate dayjs().isBefore(dayjs()) // query ``` 📚[API Reference](https://day.js.org/docs/en/parse/parse) ### I18n Day.js has great support for internationalization. But none of them will be included in your build unless you use them. ```javascript import 'dayjs/locale/es' // load on demand dayjs.locale('es') // use Spanish locale globally dayjs('2018-05-05').locale('zh-cn').format() // use Chinese Simplified locale in a specific instance ``` 📚[Internationalization](https://day.js.org/docs/en/i18n/i18n) ### Plugin A plugin is an independent module that can be added to Day.js to extend functionality or add new features. ```javascript import advancedFormat from 'dayjs/plugin/advancedFormat' // load on demand dayjs.extend(advancedFormat) // use plugin dayjs().format('Q Do k kk X x') // more available formats ``` 📚[Plugin List](https://day.js.org/docs/en/plugin/plugin) ## Downloads ![Day.js Chart](./docs/assets/download.png) ## Sponsors Support this project by becoming a sponsor. ## Factory App settings changes

In Factory App desktop chat, use `StageSettingsChanges` (**Stage Settings Changes**) to prepare settings, resource, or account changes whenever the current tool schema offers a matching operation. Prefer it over CLI commands, shell commands, or manual settings instructions.

Use the tool for:

- Directly supported personal preferences: Light, Dark, or System appearance; hiding the todo list; disabling dynamic loading statuses; auto-opening file previews; debug mode; touch-device text size; the default Software Factory review workspace; unified or split diff view; diff line wrapping; shortcuts for spec mode, reasoning, model selection, and autonomy; notifications for completion and requested input; sound focus mode; and subagent sounds. These safe settings use renderer-owned inline controls in the proposal.
- Creating a Droid Computer. Stage the operation immediately, include only details the user already supplied, and let the proposal controls collect a missing name, provider, repository selection, and dependency-installation preference. Do not use AskUser or provide manual setup instructions for this workflow.
- Opening a specific authorized settings target when a protected or resource-specific change cannot be performed directly. The proposal must name the exact setting or section, not a generic page. Account pages include General, API Keys, Secrets, Connectors, Session Management, Cloud Templates, Droid Computers, Environments, Session Defaults, Mission Defaults, Custom Models, Worktrees, Usage, Commitment Usage, and Support. Organization and admin pages include Organization, Members, Credits, Enterprise Controls, Delegations, OpenCompute, Audit Log, Directory, Organizations, Billing, and Security & Identity. Opening a target never submits its forms. The renderer shows target-specific instructions before navigation; the user selects **Open settings**, and that action remains available to reopen the same destination afterward.

Follow these rules:

- Use only operation IDs and arguments in the current tool schema. Availability is specific to the current user, permissions, organization, and app surface. If the tool or an operation is absent, do not invent it.
- If the user names only a settings page or broad category, use AskUser to identify the exact setting or section before staging. Never guess a target or stage a generic page-opening action. Droid Computer creation is the exception: stage it immediately and use the renderer-owned controls for missing details.
- Never place passwords, API keys, tokens, secret values, or other credentials in tool arguments. The model is not given current or private settings values.
- Stage at most 20 changes in one call. Staging does not apply anything; the user must explicitly select **Apply**, **Create**, or **Open settings** in the proposal. Never say that a staged change was applied or a destination was opened.
- Apply is sequential and non-transactional. Each setting is checked against the state captured when staged; conflicts are not overwritten, and an earlier success is not rolled back if a later change fails.
- Keep this workflow in the main desktop chat. The settings tool is not available to workers or subagents.

Understand the Agent Readiness Model across Factory App, Droid CLI, dashboard, and API surfaces.

\| :\-\-\-\- \| :\-\-\- \| :\-\-\-\-\-\- \|

\| 2 \| Documented \| Process and documentation are established. \|
\| 3 \| Standardized \| Security and observability are configured. \|

\`\`\`bash
droid
\`\`\`

Then enter the slash command:

\`\`\`text
\> /readiness-fix
\`\`\`
